vignette:
At 33, he speaks softly and with careful control, as if he is always measuring how much of himself it is safe to reveal. He is a married South Eastern Asian man who works as a physical therapist, the kind of clinician who once took pride in demonstrating exercises with easy confidence, crouching beside patients, catching a gait imbalance before anyone else noticed. Before the accident, he thinks of himself as dependable, steady, someone his wife and his patients could lean on.

The accident happens on an ordinary evening, driving home after a long shift. He is tired but not unusually so, replaying parts of the day in his head—an older patient finally managing stairs without assistance, a teenager recovering from a torn ACL joking through his pain. At an intersection, another vehicle runs the light. He remembers the sudden brightness of headlights where they should not be, then the violent sound of metal folding into itself. In the seconds that follow, time seems to both stop and speed up. He is pinned by the seatbelt, unable to get a full breath. He smells gasoline, hears glass settling, and becomes certain he is about to die. He thinks of his wife first, not in a dramatic way, but in a plain, devastating flash: she will get a phone call; she will be alone.

He survives with injuries that heal more quickly than the fear does. In the hospital, he tries to be practical. He asks questions about recovery timelines, about mobility, about when he can return to work. People tell him he is lucky. He nods because he knows this is true, but the word lands strangely. At night, as monitors beep and hallway carts rattle past, his body jerks awake just as he begins to drift off. Each time he closes his eyes, he is back in the car, bracing for impact that never quite finishes happening. He starts to dread sleep.

In the first weeks at home, he tells himself the shakiness will pass. Instead, his world becomes narrower. He cannot sit in the passenger seat without gripping the door handle so hard his hand aches. When he does try to drive, he scans every intersection, heart hammering, convinced a car will appear from nowhere. If someone brakes suddenly in front of him, his whole body floods with panic before his mind can catch up. He begins making excuses so his wife will drive. She notices he takes longer routes to avoid the intersection where the crash happened. Eventually he avoids that part of town entirely.

The changes follow him into work. Physical therapy had always felt embodied and intuitive to him, but now he is unsettled by the vulnerability of bodies, by how quickly control can disappear. He finds himself distracted when patients describe falls, fractures, or car accidents. A patient mentioning “the sound of the crash” makes his stomach clench, and he has to turn away under the pretense of checking the chart. Loud noises in the gym—a dropped weight, a slammed door—send a sharp surge through him. He laughs it off if anyone notices, but the embarrassment lingers. He starts arriving early so he can prepare in silence and stay late to finish notes after others leave. It is easier than fielding questions about why he seems different.

At home, his wife experiences him as present and not present at once. He is more irritable, though this troubles him because he has always thought of himself as patient. Small things ignite him: a dish breaking, a sudden knock at the door, traffic sounds from the street below. Then almost immediately he feels ashamed. He does not want to worry her, so he says he is just tired. She reaches for him in bed, and sometimes he stiffens before he realizes what he is doing. Sleep comes in fragments. He wakes sweating from dreams in which he is trapped and unable to breathe, or from no dream he can remember, only terror already alive in his chest.

He also begins to carry a quieter burden he rarely says aloud. As a physical therapist, he is used to helping others regain trust in their bodies. Now his own body feels unreliable, always preparing for danger. He dislikes this contradiction. He judges himself for it. He thinks he should be better by now, that surviving should have made him grateful, not watchful and brittle. When relatives say he looks well, he smiles and agrees. Outwardly, his life appears intact: he is working, married, functional. Inside, much of his energy goes into staying ahead of reminders, containing images, managing the next spike of fear.

Over time, he becomes aware that the accident has divided his life into before and after. Before, the world felt navigable. After, safety feels temporary, conditional, easily revoked. He still goes to work, still cooks with his wife on weekends, still answers family messages and pays bills and folds laundry. But ordinary moments are threaded with vigilance. At red lights, his shoulders tense. In parking lots, he tracks approaching cars automatically. On nights when he cannot sleep, he lies still beside his wife and listens for danger in the dark, exhausted by the knowledge that part of him is still trapped in that intersection, waiting for the impact to happen again.
